home.title: Internal Tool Platform Assessment
home.intro: This assessment pairs a working prototype of the three Power Apps workloads with an evaluation of what replacing the platform would take, and concludes with a recommendation.
home.tryIt: To compare role behavior, switch between Viewer, Approver, and Admin in the top-right.
home.assessmentIntro: The analysis behind the recommendation, in three parts: research, evaluation, and recommendation.
home.prototypeNote: Prototype note: data is stored in memory and reseeds on restart; this scope decision is discussed in the evaluation.
home.researchDescription: What Power Apps provides, and which capabilities the three apps rely on.
home.evaluationDescription: What the prototype replicated, what it didn't, and what closing the gap would cost.
home.recommendationDescription: The build-vs-buy recommendation and the reasoning behind it.

gaps.title: What Was Not, and the Gap
gaps.intro: Not replicated, and what bridging each gap would take.

sso.name: Real SSO
sso.takes: Managed provider (Auth0, Clerk, WorkOS). Days to integrate, permanent dependency.

database.name: Persistent database
database.takes: Postgres plus migrations, backups, retention. Days to set up, ongoing operations.

connectors.name: Connectors
connectors.takes: Hand-built integrations or an integration layer (Composio, Merge, Paragon). The hardest gap: ongoing work either way.

citizen.name: Citizen development
citizen.takes: Every new tool and every change becomes an engineering ticket.

compliance.name: Compliance certification
compliance.takes: Inherited from infrastructure choices; months of audit work if certification is required.

build.title: Build cost
build.body: Engineering hours first: hardening the prototype into a production system (SSO, database, integrations, testing) is weeks of senior time, not hours. And building still means buying: workflow engines (Temporal, Inngest), managed auth, integration layers each have a bill. Self-hosting the open-source equivalents trades subscriptions for cloud spend. There is no zero-vendor option.

maintenance.title: Maintenance burden
maintenance.body: Connectors are a product, not a feature; someone must keep every integration working as third-party APIs change. Self-hosted infrastructure adds patching, upgrades, and on-call.

security.title: Security implications
security.body: Authentication and authorization are a permanent commitment. Authentication (SSO, sessions, MFA) and authorization (role models, permission checks on every action) come with the platform today and would become the team's responsibility. In a regulated fintech, so do audit and compliance obligations.

opportunity.title: Opportunity cost
opportunity.body: Citizen development disappears: operations and compliance stop building their own apps and file tickets instead. Demand forecast decides the scale: at three to ten CRUD apps the current team absorbs it; beyond that, one to three dedicated engineers at $200K+ exceed the license cost before opportunity cost is counted.

capexOpex.title: Capex vs. Opex
capexOpex.intro: How the dimensions land as one-time versus recurring cost.

build.capex: Initial build: weeks of senior engineering to harden the prototype
build.opex: Tool subscriptions or cloud spend for self-hosted equivalents

security.opex: Access reviews, dependency patching, audit and compliance work

opportunity.capex: Features not shipped during the initial build
opportunity.opex: Every tool change as an engineering ticket; 1 to 3 dedicated engineers ($200K+ each) if demand grows

capexOpex.buyProfile: Buying inverts the profile: near-zero capex, a single opex line (the license), and the vendor carries maintenance and security.
